issues.legal_issue: Time spent pursuing a remedy to set aside an ex parte decree may constitute sufficient cause to condone delay in a subsequent appeal against the decree when the remedies were pursued consecutively in good faith and without dilatory conduct or gross negligence.
material_facts: A partition suit resulted in an ex parte preliminary decree.
The defendants first applied to set aside the decree; that application was dismissed on its merits, and they appealed against the dismissal.
After that appeal had remained pending for about three years, they withdrew it and filed an appeal against the ex parte decree the following day, seeking condonation of delay.
The courts found no gross negligence in pursuing the matter, and the defendants would otherwise lose the opportunity to challenge the preliminary decree on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The time spent pursuing the set-aside remedy constituted sufficient cause on these facts. The delay in filing the appeal against the ex parte decree was condoned, and the appeal was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits a liberal construction of “sufficient cause” to advance substantial justice where inaction, negligence, or lack of bona fides is not attributable to the litigant. The right of appeal under Section 96(2) CPC is statutory, and Section 97 CPC makes an appeal against a preliminary decree important because its correctness may not later be disputed in an appeal from the final decree. Order IX Rule 13 and Section 96(2) provide distinct remedies; consecutive pursuit is not automatically barred, although delay may be refused where the litigant used dilatory tactics or lacked bona fides. The Court relied on B. Madhuri Goud v. B. Damodar Reddy and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy on sufficient cause and limitation, and Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar on the statutory appeal right.

rule.if: appeal_against_ex_parte_decree and prior_set_aside_proceeding and prior_proceeding_caused_delay and bona_fide_pursuit and no_dilatory_tactics and no_gross_negligence

predicates.appeal_against_ex_parte_decree: The litigant filed an appeal challenging a decree entered in the litigant’s absence.
predicates.prior_set_aside_proceeding: The litigant first pursued a proceeding seeking to set aside that decree.
predicates.prior_proceeding_caused_delay: The time spent pursuing the earlier proceeding contributed to the delay in filing the appeal against the decree.
predicates.bona_fide_pursuit: The litigant pursued the available remedies in good faith.
predicates.no_dilatory_tactics: The litigant did not use the proceedings to delay the opposing party’s case.
predicates.no_gross_negligence: The litigant was not grossly negligent in pursuing the matter.
predicates.delay_condoned: The delay in filing the appeal is excused.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an ex parte decree, a prior set-aside proceeding caused delay, and the remedies were pursued in good faith without dilatory tactics or gross negligence, the delay is excused.

issues.legal_issue: Dismissal on the merits of an application to set aside an ex parte decree does not bar a regular appeal challenging the decree on its merits.
material_facts: The defendants’ application to set aside the ex parte decree was dismissed on its merits.
The defendants subsequently filed a regular appeal challenging the ex parte decree itself.
issues.conclusion: The regular appeal under Section 96(2) CPC is not barred merely because the application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC was dismissed on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Order IX Rule 13 CPC concerns whether summons were duly served or whether sufficient cause prevented the defendant from appearing; Section 96(2) CPC permits an appeal from an original ex parte decree and allows the appellate court to examine the decree on its merits. The statutory right of appeal cannot be curtailed without express statutory language or necessary implication. Under Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar, dismissal of an Order IX Rule 13 application does not prevent a first appeal on the merits, although the appellant cannot use that appeal to relitigate the grounds concerning the ex parte hearing addressed by that application. The Court also referred to Deepal Girishbhai Soni v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. and Chandravathi P.K. v. C.K. Saji on the statutory nature of appeal rights.

predicates.appeal_against_ex_parte_decree: The litigant filed a regular appeal challenging a decree entered in the litigant’s absence.
predicates.set_aside_application_dismissed_on_merit: The court dismissed on its merits the litigant’s application seeking to set aside that decree.
predicates.regular_appeal_not_barred: The regular appeal remains available and is not barred by dismissal of the set-aside application.

issues.definition: When a litigant appeals an ex parte decree after the set-aside application has been dismissed on its merits, the regular appeal is not barred.
